body:
**Case: Lancet Ghana.** Lancet Ghana is a small medical centre situated within the congestion zone of Accra, providing laboratory diagnostics for the people of Chorkor. It started as a sole trader in early 2012, and facilitates timely, cost-effective and high-quality diagnostic care in a safe and secure environment, with advisory services given by a team of Biomedical/Medical Laboratory Scientists. Its laboratory department employs sophisticated, high-throughput equipment; all general clinical laboratory tests are performed in-house, and as a National Laboratory guideline specific tests are sent to local partners such as Korle Bu Teaching Hospital. As the new manager you have noticed a few challenges within the environment in which the business is located, and are considering drastic changes.

**Swagga Papa**, a notorious employee and habitual late comer, does not understand how the environment is relevant to his laboratory activities. *"My job is very simple, I take samples from clients, run these samples and give them the report."*

**As a professional laboratory scientist, explain to Swagga Papa the relevance of the environment to his work. Your explanation must consider both forces within and without the business environment.**
answer:
> [!answer]
> Every organisation is an **open system**: it takes inputs from its environment, transforms them and returns outputs to it. Swagga Papa's work therefore cannot be insulated from the environment.
>
> **A. Internal environment (forces within)** — factors the business largely controls:
> | Force | Relevance to his work |
> |---|---|
> | **Owners/management and objectives** | Set the policies, turnaround times and quality standards he must meet |
> | **Employees and organisational culture** | His lateness affects colleagues' workload, morale and teamwork; culture sets attitudes to punctuality and quality |
> | **Organisational structure and resources** | Who he reports to, how specimens flow, the staffing levels available |
> | **Equipment, reagents and physical resources** | High-throughput analysers, reagent stocks and maintenance determine whether he can test at all |
> | **Quality management system** | SOPs, internal quality control, calibration and safety rules govern how every sample is handled |
>
> **B. External environment (forces without)**
> *Task (micro) environment* — those he deals with directly:
> | Force | Relevance |
> |---|---|
> | **Clients/patients of Chorkor** | Their numbers, needs, ability to pay and satisfaction determine the workload and the centre's survival |
> | **Clinicians who request tests** | Their trust depends on accuracy and turnaround; about 70% of medical decisions rest on laboratory results |
> | **Suppliers of reagents and equipment** | Late or poor-quality supply halts testing; prices affect cost |
> | **Partner/referral laboratories (e.g. Korle Bu)** | Specific tests must be referred; their performance affects his reports |
> | **Competitors** | Other laboratories in Accra set the standard for price, speed and service |
>
> *General (macro) environment* — PESTEL forces affecting everyone:
> | Force | Relevance |
> |---|---|
> | **Political/legal** | National Laboratory guidelines, licensing and accreditation, health and labour law, the **congestion-zone regulations** affecting the premises |
> | **Economic** | Inflation and exchange rates raise reagent costs; clients' incomes affect demand; NHIS reimbursement |
> | **Socio-cultural** | Health-seeking behaviour, literacy, beliefs and trust in laboratory testing in Chorkor |
> | **Technological** | New analysers, LIS/IT systems, molecular methods — he must keep learning or become obsolete |
> | **Ecological/physical** | Congestion, power supply, waste disposal, temperature control for reagents |
>
> **Conclusion for Swagga Papa:** his 'simple' job of taking, running and reporting samples depends at every step on reagents arriving, equipment working, power being available, guidelines being followed, clients continuing to come and clinicians continuing to trust the results — and **his own punctuality is itself an internal environmental factor** affecting turnaround, colleagues and the centre's reputation and survival, and therefore his own job.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The business environment is conventionally analysed in three layers: the **internal environment** (owners, employees, culture, structure, resources — controllable), the **task/micro environment** (customers, suppliers, competitors, intermediaries, regulators — influenceable), and the **general/macro environment** (PESTEL — uncontrollable but must be monitored). An **open-systems** view shows why no job inside the organisation is independent of these layers: inputs, process and outputs all cross the boundary. SWOT analysis links the layers — internal **strengths and weaknesses** against external **opportunities and threats** — and is the basis of the 'drastic changes' the new manager is considering.

## Simplified explanation

His job depends on things **inside** the business (management, colleagues, equipment, reagents, rules) and **outside** it (patients, doctors, suppliers, partner labs, competitors, government rules, the economy, technology and the congested location). If any of them changes, his work changes — and his own lateness is itself one of those internal factors.
hint: Internal, task and general (PESTEL) environments — and link each to his bench work.

body: **Curtis**, another employee of Lancet Ghana, is not sure **who to report to** at work. He believes there must be an order of reporting or some sort of line of command. As the manager, use an illustration to explain the **three levels of management** to Curtis and how they contribute to organisational effectiveness.
answer:
> [!answer]
> The levels form a **pyramid**, narrow at the top and wide at the base:
>
> ```
>              ┌───────────────────────────┐
>              │   TOP (strategic) level    │  ← few managers
>              │  MD/CEO, Board, Director   │
>              ├───────────────────────────┤
>              │   MIDDLE (tactical) level  │
>              │ Lab Manager, Head of Dept  │
>              ├───────────────────────────┤
>              │  LOWER (operational) level │  ← many managers
>              │ Supervisors, Section Heads │
>              ├───────────────────────────┤
>              │   Non-managerial staff     │
>              │  (Curtis, Swagga Papa…)    │
>              └───────────────────────────┘
> ```
>
> | Level | Who | Role | Contribution to effectiveness |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | **Top (strategic)** | Owner/CEO/Managing Director, Board | Set the **vision, mission, objectives and long-term strategy**; relate the organisation to its environment; commit major resources; represent the organisation externally | Gives the whole organisation **direction and purpose**, and secures the resources and legitimacy it needs to survive |
> | **Middle (tactical)** | Laboratory Manager, Heads of Department/Unit | **Translate top-level strategy into departmental plans, budgets and targets**; organise and co-ordinate sections; channel information up and down | Acts as the **link** that converts strategy into action and feeds operational reality back up; co-ordinates between departments |
> | **Lower (operational/first-line)** | Supervisors, section heads, shift leaders | **Direct and supervise the day-to-day work** of non-managerial staff; allocate tasks, maintain quality and discipline, solve immediate problems | Ensures the work is **actually done correctly, on time and to standard** — where quality and turnaround are won or lost |
>
> **Answer to Curtis's question:** he reports to his **immediate supervisor at the lower/operational level**, who reports to the **middle-level manager (Head of Department/Laboratory Manager)**, who in turn reports to **top management**. This is the **scalar chain/chain of command**, and following it gives **unity of command** — one boss per employee — so that instructions are consistent, accountability is clear and problems are escalated in an orderly way.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The levels differ not only in authority but in the **mix of managerial skills** required (Katz): lower-level managers need mostly **technical** skills, middle managers a balance, and top managers predominantly **conceptual** skills, with **human/interpersonal** skills important at every level. They also differ in time horizon (shift-to-week, month-to-year, several years) and in decision type (programmed/operational versus non-programmed/strategic). The **scalar chain** with **unity of command** (Fayol) prevents conflicting instructions and divided accountability; the **span of control** determines how tall or flat the pyramid is.

## Simplified explanation

There are three layers: **top managers** decide where the business is going, **middle managers** turn that into departmental plans, and **first-line supervisors** run the daily work. Curtis reports to his **supervisor**, who reports to the **head of department**, who reports to the **top**.
hint: Top, middle, lower — plus the chain of command and unity of command.

body: The style adopted by a leader has very important implications for the effectiveness of the leader himself, the level of employee cooperation and the success and survival of the group. **Explain, with relevant examples, the three styles that can be adopted by a leader in executing his duties.**
answer:
> [!answer]
> Lewin's three classical leadership styles:
>
> | Style | Description | Example in the laboratory | When appropriate |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | **1. Autocratic (authoritarian)** | The leader **makes decisions alone**, dictates methods, gives orders and expects obedience; communication is downward; power is centralised; motivation by reward and punishment | The manager unilaterally fixes the duty roster and insists tests are run his way, disciplining Swagga Papa for lateness | **Crises and emergencies**, inexperienced or undisciplined staff, where decisions must be fast or safety is at stake |
> | **2. Democratic (participative)** | The leader **involves subordinates in decision-making**, consults, delegates and encourages discussion, but retains final responsibility; two-way communication | The manager holds a staff meeting on how to cut turnaround time and adopts the team's proposal | **Skilled, motivated professionals**; where commitment and quality of decision matter and time permits — usually the best general style |
> | **3. Laissez-faire (free-rein/delegative)** | The leader gives **minimal direction**, provides resources and lets subordinates set their own goals and methods; hands-off supervision | Experienced senior scientists are left to organise and validate a new molecular assay themselves | **Highly skilled, self-motivated experts**; research and creative work. It fails with inexperienced or undisciplined staff — who then drift |
>
> **Implications:** the autocratic style gets quick compliance but **lowers morale, initiative and retention**; the democratic style raises **satisfaction, cooperation and the quality of decisions** but is slower; laissez-faire can produce excellent work from experts but **chaos and low output** from staff who need direction. The effective leader is **contingent** — matching the style to the task, the maturity of the followers and the situation.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Lewin, Lippitt and White's experiments found that democratic leadership produced work of the highest quality and the best group relations, autocratic leadership produced the greatest **quantity** but only while the leader was present, and laissez-faire produced the least and the poorest work. Later theory made style **contingent**: Tannenbaum and Schmidt's continuum of boss-centred to subordinate-centred behaviour; Fiedler's contingency model (task- versus relationship-motivated leaders matched to situational favourableness); and Hersey and Blanchard's **situational leadership** (telling, selling, participating, delegating according to follower readiness). Transformational leadership adds vision, inspiration and individual consideration to the picture.

## Simplified explanation

**Autocratic** — the leader decides and gives orders. **Democratic** — the leader consults the team and decides together. **Laissez-faire** — the leader leaves the team to get on with it. Each works in a different situation: orders in an emergency, consultation with skilled staff, hands-off with experts.
hint: Autocratic, democratic, laissez-faire — with examples and when each fits.

body: Comparing **monetary and non-monetary forms of compensation**, which is **most effective in motivating employees** in the laboratory?
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Both are needed, but non-monetary compensation is generally the more effective and durable motivator of professional laboratory staff — provided monetary compensation is already fair and adequate.**
>
> | | Monetary compensation | Non-monetary compensation |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Examples** | Salary, allowances, overtime, bonuses, commissions, pension and medical cover | Recognition and praise, training and career development, promotion, job enrichment and responsibility, flexible hours, good working conditions, safety, participation in decisions, awards, job security |
> | **Effect** | Removes dissatisfaction; attracts and retains staff; immediate but **short-lived** effect — people quickly adapt to a pay rise | Satisfies **esteem, achievement, growth and self-actualisation** needs; effect is **longer lasting** and builds commitment |
> | **Cost** | Recurrent and expensive for a small centre like Lancet Ghana | Mostly **low cost**, within the manager's control |
>
> **Justification (Herzberg's two-factor theory):** pay, conditions, supervision and job security are **hygiene factors** — their absence causes dissatisfaction, but their presence does not, by itself, motivate. True **motivators** are achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement and growth — all non-monetary. Equally, by **Maslow**, once physiological and safety needs are met by an adequate salary, people are driven by belonging, esteem and self-actualisation.
>
> **Practical conclusion for the manager:** first pay a **fair, competitive and equitable wage** (an underpaid professional cannot be motivated by praise); then rely mainly on **recognition, training, career progression, responsibility and good working conditions** to motivate — and use monetary incentives selectively, for example a performance bonus tied to turnaround time or quality.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The evidence is that money functions well as a **hygiene factor and as a signal of recognition**, but poorly as a sustained motivator: its effect decays rapidly (hedonic adaptation), it can **crowd out intrinsic motivation** for professional work, and perceived **inequity** in pay (Adams' equity theory) is a powerful demotivator regardless of absolute level. **Expectancy theory** (Vroom) adds that any reward — monetary or not — motivates only if the employee believes effort leads to performance, performance leads to the reward, and the reward is valued. For a small laboratory with limited funds, the practical lever is therefore job design, recognition and development, resting on a base of fair pay.

## Simplified explanation

Pay must be **fair first** — otherwise nothing else works. But beyond that, what really keeps laboratory staff motivated is **recognition, training, promotion, responsibility and good working conditions**, which also cost the business far less.

body: **Why is the study of management important to a laboratory scientist?**
answer:
> [!answer]
> 1. **Laboratory scientists become managers.** With experience a scientist is appointed section head, laboratory manager or director, and will then be required to **plan, organise, staff, lead and control** — skills that are not taught by the science itself.
> 2. **Quality and accuracy depend on management.** About **70% of medical decisions are based on laboratory tests**; quality is determined by how the laboratory is organised and managed — SOPs, quality control, calibration, documentation, staff competence and workflow.
> 3. **Efficient use of scarce resources** — budgeting, procurement, inventory and reagent stock control, equipment maintenance and cost containment all require management knowledge.
> 4. **Managing people** — recruiting, training, scheduling, motivating, appraising and disciplining staff (a Swagga Papa must be managed), and working effectively within a multidisciplinary team.
> 5. **Understanding the organisation and its environment** — how the laboratory fits into the hospital and the health system, and how political, economic, legal and technological changes affect it.
> 6. **Entrepreneurship** — many scientists establish their own diagnostic centres and must understand business ownership, finance, marketing and regulation.
> 7. **Better followership and communication** — even as a bench scientist, understanding management makes one a more effective team member who grasps why decisions are taken and can contribute to improvement.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Management is the process of **achieving organisational objectives efficiently and effectively through and with other people**, by means of the functions of planning, organising, staffing, leading and controlling, applied to human, financial, physical and informational resources. In the laboratory these functions have specific technical expressions: planning becomes test menu and capacity planning; organising becomes workflow and section design; controlling becomes **quality control, quality assurance and accreditation (ISO 15189)**. The scientist who understands both the technical and the managerial dimension can therefore bridge them — which is why laboratory management is a core component of medical laboratory science curricula.

## Simplified explanation

Because a laboratory scientist will sooner or later have to **run a laboratory** — managing people, money, equipment and quality — and because the accuracy of the results depends as much on **how the lab is managed** as on the science itself.
hint: Think of what happens when a scientist is promoted, and of what quality depends on.

body: **What is planning**, and mention **two (2) reasons** why it is important to plan.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Planning** is the **primary management function of deciding in advance what is to be done, when, how and by whom** — setting objectives and formulating the courses of action, policies, procedures, programmes and budgets needed to achieve them. It bridges the gap between **where the organisation is now and where it wants to be**, and is future-oriented and decision-based.
>
> **Two reasons why planning is important**
> 1. **It provides direction and a sense of purpose** — everyone knows the objectives and how their work contributes, so effort is co-ordinated rather than duplicated or contradictory.
> 2. **It provides the standards for control** — performance can only be measured against a predetermined plan; without objectives and targets there is nothing to control against.
>
> Other acceptable reasons: it **reduces uncertainty and risk** by anticipating change; it promotes **efficient use of scarce resources** and reduces waste and overlapping activity; it **facilitates decision-making**; it encourages **innovation and creativity**; and it motivates staff by setting clear, achievable targets.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Planning is the **first and the pervasive** management function, because organising, staffing, leading and controlling all implement a plan. It proceeds through setting objectives, scanning the environment (SWOT/PESTEL), identifying and evaluating alternative courses of action, selecting one, formulating derivative plans and budgets, and reviewing. Plans are classified by **level** (strategic, tactical, operational), by **time** (long, medium, short term) and by **use** — **single-use** (programmes, projects, budgets) versus **standing** (policies, procedures, rules). Its limitations are the cost and time it consumes, the rigidity it can create, and the unreliability of forecasts in a turbulent environment.

## Simplified explanation

Planning is **deciding ahead of time what to do, how, when and by whom**. It matters because it **gives everyone direction** and because it **sets the targets you later measure performance against**.
hint: Deciding in advance — and what control needs in order to work.

body: Explain **two (2) types of planning** that managers practise in running a successful business.
answer:
> [!answer]
> | Type | Who does it | Time horizon | Nature |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | **1. Strategic planning** | **Top management** | **Long term — 3 to 5 years and beyond** | Defines the **vision, mission and overall objectives** of the whole organisation and how it will relate to its environment; broad, directional and concerned with *what business we are in* and *how we will compete*. Example: Lancet Ghana deciding to open branches outside the Accra congestion zone and to add molecular diagnostics. |
> | **2. Tactical planning** | **Middle management** | **Medium term — about 1 to 3 years** | **Translates the strategic plan into departmental plans, budgets and targets**; decides the resources each unit needs and how it will contribute. Example: the laboratory manager planning equipment purchase, staffing and the test menu for the new branch. |
> | **3. Operational planning** | **Lower/first-line management** | **Short term — daily, weekly, monthly, up to a year** | Specific, detailed plans for **day-to-day activities** — duty rosters, reagent orders, workflow schedules, standard operating procedures. |
>
> (Any two explained. **Contingency planning** — preparing alternative courses of action for foreseeable emergencies such as equipment breakdown or a power failure — is also acceptable, as are the **single-use/standing plan** and **long-/short-range** classifications.)
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The three levels of plan correspond to the three levels of management and form a **hierarchy of ends and means**: each lower-level plan is the *means* to the level above and the *end* for the level below, so that departmental targets aggregate into corporate objectives. Plans are also classified by **frequency of use** — **single-use plans** (programmes, projects and budgets, for a non-recurring purpose) and **standing plans** (policies, procedures and rules, for recurring situations) — and by **specificity** (directional versus specific). Effective planning requires that the three levels be **integrated and consistent**, which is the chief task of the middle manager.

## Simplified explanation

**Strategic** — top managers decide the long-term direction of the whole business. **Tactical** — middle managers turn that into departmental plans and budgets for the next year or two. **Operational** — supervisors plan the day-to-day work.
hint: Strategic, tactical, operational — pick two and say who does each and over what period.

body: Describe the **four (4) types of skills** that managers in the laboratory need in performing their duties.
answer:
> [!answer]
> | Skill | What it is | In the laboratory |
> |---|---|---|
> | **1. Technical skills** | Knowledge of and proficiency in a **specialised field, its methods, procedures and equipment** | Performing and troubleshooting assays, operating and calibrating analysers, interpreting quality-control data, knowing the SOPs. Most important at the **lower/first-line** level |
> | **2. Human (interpersonal) skills** | The ability to **work with, understand, communicate with, motivate and lead people**, individually and in groups | Supervising bench staff, resolving conflict, motivating a late-comer, counselling clients, working in a multidisciplinary team. Equally important at **all levels** |
> | **3. Conceptual skills** | The ability to **see the organisation as a whole**, to think abstractly and strategically, to understand how the parts fit together and how the organisation relates to its environment | Deciding the laboratory's test menu and expansion strategy, analysing how regulation or exchange rates will affect the centre. Most important at the **top** level |
> | **4. Diagnostic and analytical (decision/problem-solving) skills** | The ability to **investigate a problem, determine its cause and design an appropriate response**, using data and judgement | Identifying why turnaround time has lengthened or why QC is drifting, analysing the options and choosing a remedy |
>
> Other acceptable skills in some texts: **communication skills**, **time-management skills**, **political skills** and **design skills**.
>
> **Note:** the **mix** changes with the level of management — technical skills dominate at the bottom of the pyramid, conceptual skills at the top, while human skills are needed in roughly equal measure throughout.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Robert Katz's classic 1974 paper identified **technical, human and conceptual** skills and showed that their relative importance varies with managerial level — the most important practical implication being that **promoting the best bench scientist does not automatically produce a good manager**, because the skill mix required changes. Later writers added **diagnostic/analytical** skills and sometimes **political** and **communication** skills. For a laboratory, failure of conceptual skill shows as a technically excellent unit that is out of step with the health system; failure of human skill shows as high staff turnover and poor teamwork; failure of technical skill shows as a manager who cannot evaluate the work he supervises.

## Simplified explanation

**Technical** — knowing how the tests and machines work. **Human** — getting on with and leading people. **Conceptual** — seeing the whole organisation and its place in the bigger picture. **Diagnostic/analytical** — working out what the real problem is and how to fix it.
hint: Katz's three, plus the problem-solving one.

body:
A pregnant woman comes for HIV testing. Your test site has just run out of the **2nd test in the algorithm**. You tell her that she will have to come back in 2 days. She becomes very emotional and explains that she has travelled a long distance after finally deciding to get tested and will not be back in the area for a long time. Feeling sorry for her, you proceed to perform **test one only**, and report a **resulting positive test to the client**.

**Explain the implication of this action on your business reputation.**
answer:
> [!answer]
> **The action is professionally and ethically wrong**: the national HIV testing algorithm requires a **sequence of tests**, and a single reactive screening test is only a **presumptive (screen-reactive)** result, never a diagnosis. Reporting it as positive is reporting an **unconfirmed result**.
>
> **Implications for the business reputation**
> 1. **A false-positive diagnosis.** Screening assays have high sensitivity but imperfect specificity; in a pregnant woman at low prior risk the **predictive value positive of a single test is poor**, so the result may well be wrong. The consequences — psychological trauma, stigma, marital breakdown, possibly unnecessary ARVs or even a decision about the pregnancy — are catastrophic and will be traced back to the laboratory.
> 2. **Loss of credibility and trust.** Clinicians and clients rely on the centre for accurate results; once a wrong HIV result becomes known, **trust in every other test the laboratory issues is undermined**.
> 3. **Negative word of mouth.** In a small community such as Chorkor, news of a wrong HIV result spreads rapidly; clients will go elsewhere, revenue falls and the centre's survival is threatened.
> 4. **Legal liability and regulatory sanction.** The centre and the scientist may face a **negligence claim**, disciplinary action by the professional body, and sanction or loss of licence/accreditation for breaching the **National Laboratory guidelines**.
> 5. **Loss of partnerships and contracts** — referral partners (such as Korle Bu), the NHIS, NGOs and the national HIV programme may withdraw from a laboratory that does not follow protocol.
> 6. **Internal effects** — it sets a precedent that **protocols may be bypassed out of sympathy**, eroding the quality culture and inviting further errors.
>
> **What should have been done:** explain honestly that **only a screening test can be performed today and that it cannot confirm HIV status**; record the result as screen-reactive/inconclusive pending confirmation; arrange confirmation by **referring her, the same day, to a partner site** that has the full algorithm, or take and store a specimen for testing when reagents arrive; give pre- and post-test counselling; link her to antenatal/PMTCT services; and report the stock-out so that it does not recur.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

This is a question about **quality management and reputation as a business asset**. HIV testing uses a serial algorithm precisely because **predictive value positive depends on prevalence and on the combined specificity of the tests**: a single assay with 99% specificity used in a population with 2% prevalence yields roughly as many false positives as true positives. Departing from the algorithm therefore converts a technically valid screen into a clinically invalid diagnosis. In service businesses, quality is judged largely by **outcome credibility**; the standard marketing observation is that dissatisfied clients tell far more people than satisfied ones, and in diagnostics a single publicised error can be fatal to the enterprise. Sympathy is not a defence — the correct response to a stock-out is **referral and honest communication**, not a shortcut.

## Simplified explanation

One test is not enough to say someone has HIV. Reporting it as positive could be **completely wrong**, with devastating consequences for her — and when that comes out, **nobody will trust the laboratory again**, clients will leave, and the centre may face legal action and lose its licence.
hint: What does a single test in an algorithm actually prove, and what happens when the result is wrong?

body: About **70% of medical decisions are based on laboratory tests**. Thus the quality and accuracy of tests is of vital importance, and quality is very much related to the manner in which the laboratory is **organised and managed**. Explain how the laboratory manager will **organise the laboratory using the five (5) structural components**.
answer:
> [!answer]
> Using Mintzberg's five basic parts of the organisation, applied to the laboratory:
>
> | Component | Who/what it is in the laboratory | How the manager organises it |
> |---|---|---|
> | **1. Strategic apex** | The **laboratory director/top management** (and owners) | Sets the vision, quality policy and objectives; secures resources and licences; relates the laboratory to the hospital, regulators and the health system |
> | **2. Middle line** | **Heads of department/section** — haematology, chemical pathology, microbiology, serology | Translate policy into sectional plans, budgets and rosters; supervise and link the apex to the bench; report performance upward |
> | **3. Operating core** | The **bench scientists, technicians, phlebotomists and assistants** who do the actual testing | Grouped into sections by discipline or by workflow; given clear SOPs, competencies, training and defined roles; workload balanced and shifts rostered |
> | **4. Technostructure** | The **quality manager, safety officer, QC/QA and laboratory information (LIS) staff**, method-validation and standardisation staff | Design and standardise the work — SOPs, internal and external quality control, calibration schedules, document control, audit and accreditation (ISO 15189) |
> | **5. Support staff** | **Stores and procurement, maintenance/biomedical engineering, cleaning, transport, reception, records, accounts, IT** | Provide the services the core depends on — reagent supply and stock control, equipment servicing, specimen transport, waste disposal, billing |
>
> In organising, the manager must also settle the **organising principles that bind these parts**: **division of work and specialisation**, **departmentation** (by discipline or workflow), **delegation of authority with corresponding responsibility**, the **chain of command with unity of command**, an appropriate **span of control**, and the degree of **centralisation versus decentralisation** — all documented in an **organisational chart and job descriptions** so that, as Curtis asked, everyone knows who reports to whom.
>
> *(An equally acceptable answer uses the five structural elements of organisational design: **work specialisation, departmentation, chain of command, span of control, and centralisation/formalisation**.)*
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Mintzberg's framework is useful in a laboratory because it separates **those who do the work** (operating core) from **those who standardise it** (technostructure) and **those who service it** (support staff) — a distinction that matters greatly for quality, since laboratory quality is achieved principally by **standardisation of work processes** (SOPs, QC, calibration, competency assessment), the technostructure's co-ordinating mechanism. A laboratory is in fact close to Mintzberg's **professional bureaucracy**: a large, highly trained operating core with substantial autonomy, standardisation by **skills and qualifications** as well as by process, a relatively thin middle line and a well-developed support staff. Organising decisions — how to departmentalise, how wide a span of control, how much to decentralise — then determine whether that core can deliver accurate, timely results.

## Simplified explanation

Five parts: the **director at the top**, the **heads of section in the middle**, the **bench staff who do the testing**, the **quality and safety people who write and check the procedures**, and the **support services** (stores, maintenance, IT, reception). The manager must define each part, who reports to whom, and how they work together.
hint: Top, middle, the people doing the work, the people standardising it, and the people supporting it.

body: Deciding on the **form of business ownership** has always been a challenge in establishing and running a business. Explain the **three forms of business ownership**, stating their **advantages and disadvantages**.
answer:
> [!answer]
> | | **Sole proprietorship** | **Partnership** | **Company (corporation)** |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | **Nature** | Owned and run by **one person**, who is the business (e.g. Lancet Ghana at its start in 2012) | Association of **2–20 persons** carrying on business in common with a view to profit, under a partnership deed | A **separate legal person** registered under the Companies Act, owned by shareholders and run by directors; private or public, limited by shares or guarantee |
> | **Advantages** | Easy and cheap to form; **owner takes all the profit**; full control and quick decisions; secrecy; easy to dissolve; minimal legal formality | **More capital and skills** than one person; shared workload and risk; relatively easy to form; combined judgement; some secrecy retained | **Limited liability**; **separate legal personality** — can sue, be sued and own property; **perpetual succession**; can raise large capital by issuing shares; transferable ownership; professional management; economies of scale |
> | **Disadvantages** | **Unlimited liability** — personal assets at risk; **limited capital** and difficulty borrowing; limited skills; no continuity — the business ends with the owner's death or illness; heavy workload and stress | **Unlimited liability** (except for limited partners); **each partner is liable for the others' acts**; risk of disagreement and deadlock; **no perpetual succession** — death, bankruptcy or withdrawal of a partner can dissolve it; profits shared; slower decisions | **Expensive and complex to form** and to run; heavy **legal and regulatory compliance** (audited accounts, filings, meetings); **double taxation** in some systems; loss of secrecy through published accounts; **separation of ownership from control** can create agency problems; slower decision-making |
>
> **Choosing between them** depends on the capital required, the liability exposure (high in diagnostic work), the tax position, the need for continuity, the degree of control wanted and the cost of formation — which is why many successful sole proprietorships such as Lancet Ghana eventually **incorporate as limited liability companies** as they grow.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The decisive legal distinction is **separate legal personality** (*Salomon v Salomon*): a registered company is a person in law distinct from its members, which produces **limited liability** and **perpetual succession** and makes external equity finance possible — at the cost of formality, disclosure and regulation. Sole traders and ordinary partnerships are not separate persons, so the owners' **personal assets stand behind the business debts**; for a medical laboratory, where a negligence claim can be very large, this is a material risk and a strong argument for incorporation. Other considerations are taxation (personal income tax versus corporate tax), the ease of bringing in and retiring owners, and the cost of compliance relative to the size of the business.

## Simplified explanation

**Sole trader** — one owner, easy and all the profit is yours, but you are personally liable for everything and it ends when you do. **Partnership** — more money and skills, but you are liable for your partners' mistakes and disputes are common. **Company** — limited liability, lives on after the owners and can raise big capital, but it is costly, heavily regulated and less private.
hint: Sole proprietorship, partnership, company — liability, capital and continuity are the key contrasts.

body: Identify and explain any **four (4) sources from which leaders derive their power**.
answer:
> [!answer]
> French and Raven's bases of power:
>
> | Source | Explanation | Laboratory example |
> |---|---|---|
> | **1. Legitimate (positional) power** | Power derived from the **formal position or office** a person holds in the organisational hierarchy; subordinates accept that the holder has the **right to command** | The laboratory manager's authority to approve the duty roster and sign reports |
> | **2. Reward power** | The ability to **give or withhold rewards** that others value — pay rises, bonuses, promotion, favourable duties, recognition, training opportunities | The manager recommending a scientist for promotion or for a workshop abroad |
> | **3. Coercive power** | The ability to **punish or impose unpleasant consequences** — reprimand, demotion, withholding of privileges, dismissal | Disciplining Swagga Papa for habitual lateness. Effective short-term but breeds fear and resentment |
> | **4. Expert power** | Power derived from **superior knowledge, skill or expertise** that others need and respect | The senior scientist whose advice on a difficult assay everyone follows, regardless of rank |
> | **5. Referent (personal/charismatic) power** | Power derived from **personal qualities — admiration, respect, identification, charisma** — that makes others want to follow | The respected colleague others imitate and willingly work for |
>
> **Information power** (control of needed information) and **connection/network power** (access to influential people) are sometimes added.
>
> **Note:** legitimate, reward and coercive power are **positional** — they come with the job and are lost with it; **expert and referent power are personal** — they are earned, travel with the individual, and are the sources most consistently associated with genuine commitment rather than mere compliance.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

French and Raven's typology remains the standard. Research consistently shows that **expert and referent power produce commitment**, legitimate and reward power produce **compliance**, and coercive power produces **resistance** and only superficial conformity. Effective leaders therefore build the personal bases of power and use positional power sparingly. Power should be distinguished from **authority** (the legitimate, formally delegated right to act, which flows down the scalar chain) and from **influence** (the actual effect on others' behaviour): authority is a subset of power, and a manager may hold authority with little real power, or hold great power — as a respected expert — with no formal authority at all.

## Simplified explanation

**Legitimate** — power from the job title. **Reward** — power to give people things they want. **Coercive** — power to punish. **Expert** — power from really knowing your subject. **Referent** — power from being respected and admired.
